title: The Evening Brief: Four stories reshape sports business, law, and newsrooms
dek: Evening brings the firmest outcome yet: a federal jury held The New York Times liable for defamation for the first time in over 50 years, while tennis prize pools climb, England's Test captain opens strong, and a Seattle newsroom's editorial choice triggers a resignation.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: The New York Times lost a defamation case to Kai Spears over a falsely identified shooting witness, marking the paper's first U.S. defamation loss in over 50 years and exposing the liability gap between a factual error and a delayed correction.
bottom_line: The New York Times defamation loss to Kai Spears marks the paper's first such verdict in over 50 years and exposes the liability gap between a factual error and a delayed correction; the Times is reviewing appeal options. Tennis player leverage produced a 20 percent US Open prize increase within months of coordinated pressure, but the underlying revenue-share gap remains unresolved in the Players Advisory Council. England opened Joe Root's second captaincy with a dominant three-day Test win. Marc Stad took controlling ownership of the Timberwolves and Lynx pending league approval of expanded governance roles. Watch the Times appeal decision, the Players Advisory Council's first revenue-share moves, and whether The Seattle Times clarifies its editorial process.
body: The evening's clearest story is also the rarest: a federal jury in Tuscaloosa found The New York Times liable for defamation and false light invasion of privacy and awarded Kai Spears, a former Alabama basketball walk-on, approximately $9.25 million in damages. The verdict stems from a March 2023 article by Billy Witz that misidentified Spears as the passenger in Brandon Miller's car at the time of a fatal shooting in January 2023. The correct identification was Cooper Lee, a student manager. The Times amended the article on June 2, 2023, three months after publication, but the jury found the paper liable despite the correction. The Times has not lost a defamation lawsuit on a U.S. article in more than 50 years, according to reporting. The organization expressed disappointment at the verdict and stated it is reviewing its legal options, signaling a potential appeal.

Tennis prize pools continued their climb today as earlier reporting confirmed. The US Open will distribute $108 million in 2026, up 20 percent from the $90 million in 2025, with singles champions each receiving $5.5 million. The increase corresponds to 19.3 percent of the tournament's $559.7 million operating revenue in 2024, per the desk's reporting. The boost follows coordinated player pressure at Roland-Garros in May. The Players Advisory Council, newly established at the Slams, remains untested on whether it will produce structural changes to revenue sharing or function primarily as a communication channel while the underlying gap between current compensation (typically 15 percent of revenue) and player targets (22 percent by 2030) persists.

In cricket, England defeated Pakistan by an innings and 103 runs at Headingley in the opening Test of Joe Root's second stint as captain, concluding play on day three. Pakistan's first innings totaled 171 runs, England replied with 409, and Pakistan's second innings crumbled to 135. Harry Brook scored 91 and Root contributed 66 in England's first innings. Muhammad Usman took five wickets for 95 runs for Pakistan. Root described his team as outstanding after the win. England now leads the three-match series 1-0.

In basketball business, Marc Stad became controlling owner of the Minnesota Timberwolves and Minnesota Lynx in a transaction valued at $4.5 billion combined, the fourth-largest NBA franchise sale on record. Stad acquired the majority stake held by co-chairman Marc Lore. Co-chairman Alex Rodriguez is increasing his investment and will serve in expanded governance roles pending league approval, including co-chairman, Governor of the Lynx, and alternate Governor of the Timberwolves. The franchises include four-time NBA All-Star Anthony Edwards.

At the Seattle Times, sports columnist Matt Calkins announced his resignation on Thursday after 11 years with the paper. The departure followed the paper's decision not to publish a column Calkins submitted on July 31 titled "Agreeing with Sophie Cunningham's stance doesn't make you transphobic," which was written from the perspective of female student athletes opposed to competing against biological males. The Times told Calkins the column would not run because he had not informed editors about it in advance. Calkins stated he did not believe this explanation. The reporting does not carry the paper's fuller editorial rationale beyond the stated advance-notice requirement.
